p: Look up at night. The Moon seems close enough to touch. It is not. The Moon is about 384,000 kilometres away.

That is so far that you could line up 30 Earths between here and there. A car driving night and day would take about five months to get there. The Moon is also much smaller than Earth. It is about one quarter as wide.

v.title: Earth and the Moon to scale

pages.cap: The Moon is about one quarter as wide as Earth.
pages.fact: Did you know? Light from the Moon takes just over one second to reach your eyes.

p: Where did the Moon come from? Most scientists think it was born in a giant crash.

About 4.5 billion years ago, a world the size of Mars smashed into the young Earth. Hot rock sprayed out into space. The pieces swirled around Earth and clumped together into a ball. That ball is our Moon. Scientists still argue about the details, but the crash idea fits the Moon rocks best.
pages.cap: A huge crash, and a new moon forms from the pieces.
pages.fact: Did you know? Moon rock and Earth rock are so alike that scientists think they came from the same place.

p: The Moon looks bright, but it makes no light of its own. It is a ball of grey rock. The Sun shines on it, and the Moon bounces that sunlight to us.
Only the half facing the Sun is lit. As the Moon goes around Earth, we see different amounts of that lit half. That is why the Moon seems to change shape.
pages.cap: Sunlight always lights half the Moon. We see different slices of it.
pages.fact: Did you know? The Moon is as dark as an old road. It only looks bright next to the black sky.

opts: The Moon burns like the Sun
pages.why: The Moon is just rock. It shines because sunlight bounces off it.

p: The Moon's shapes are called phases. At new moon, the dark side faces us and we see nothing. A few nights later a thin crescent appears.
The crescent grows to a half moon, then a fat gibbous moon, then a round full moon. Then it shrinks again. The whole cycle takes about 29 and a half days. That is about one month.
pages.cap: Eight phases, going round in about a month.
pages.fact: Did you know? The word month comes from the word moon.

pages.h: You always see the same face
p: The Moon spins once for every trip it makes around Earth. So the same side always faces us. No one saw the far side until a space probe took its picture in 1959.
The Moon is covered in round holes called craters. Rocks from space crash into it and blast out bowls in the ground.

Some craters are tiny. One, near the south pole, is about 2,500 kilometres across. That is wider than the distance from Vancouver to Winnipeg. Earth gets hit too, but our air burns up most small rocks before they land.
pages.cap: A rock from space hits hard and leaves a bowl in the ground.
pages.fact: Did you know? You can see some of the Moon's big craters with just a pair of binoculars.

p: See how a crash makes a crater.
steps: Fill a tray with flour about 3 centimetres deep.
Sprinkle a thin layer of cocoa or sand on top.
Drop a marble from knee height. Look at the hole and the rays around it.
Drop it from higher up. Is the crater bigger?
Try a bigger ball. Try dropping it at an angle.
pages.cap: Flour and cocoa make craters just like the Moon's.
pages.safe: Do this outside or over a cloth, and wash your hands after.

pages.h: No air, no wind, no sound
p: The Moon has no air. There is no wind, no rain and no weather at all. Nothing wears things away.

The footprints astronauts left in 1969 are still there today. They may last for millions of years. With no air, it is also silent. And the heat is wild: about 120 degrees Celsius in the daytime, and about minus 130 at night.
pages.cap: Grey dust, black sky, and nothing moving.
pages.fact: Did you know? Without air, the sky on the Moon is black even in the daytime.

pages.q: Why do footprints on the Moon last so long?
opts: Moon dust is sticky like glue
There is no wind or rain to wear them away
pages.why: The Moon has no air, so there is no weather to wipe the footprints away.

p: For most of history, people thought the Moon was a smooth, perfect ball.

In 1609, an Italian scientist named Galileo pointed a new tool at it: a telescope. He saw mountains, valleys and craters. He drew what he saw. The Moon was a rough, rocky world, a bit like Earth. His drawings changed how people saw the sky.
pages.cap: Galileo looks at the Moon through his telescope in 1609.
pages.fact: Did you know? Galileo's telescope made the Moon look about 20 times bigger. A small telescope today can do 100 times.

p: The Moon pulls on Earth with its gravity. It pulls on the oceans too. The water on the side nearest the Moon bulges up a little, and so does the water on the far side.
As Earth spins, those bulges sweep around the world. At the beach, the sea creeps up the sand, then slides back down. These are tides. Most beaches get two high tides every day.
pages.cap: Sailors watch the tides. A boat can be stuck on the sand when the sea goes out.
pages.fact: Did you know? The Bay of Fundy in Canada has the biggest tides on Earth. The sea rises about 16 metres.

p: The Moon is small, so its gravity is weak. It pulls only one sixth as hard as Earth.
If you weigh 30 kilograms here, a scale on the Moon would show about 5. You could jump about six times higher. Astronauts found that the easiest way to move was to hop like a kangaroo.
pages.cap: A frog hopping on the Moon could go six times as far.
pages.fact: Did you know? In 1971, an astronaut hit golf balls on the Moon. His stiff spacesuit made it hard to swing, so the balls only went about 40 metres.

p: Between 1969 and 1972, twelve astronauts walked on the Moon. All of them went in Apollo spaceships. No one has been back since. The Moon is still the only other world a person has ever stood on.

pages.q: How strong is the Moon's gravity compared with Earth's?
pages.why: The Moon is much smaller than Earth, so its pull is only one sixth as strong.

p: On 20 July 1969, a spaceship called Eagle landed on the Moon. Neil Armstrong climbed down a ladder and stepped onto the dust. Buzz Aldrin followed.
The trip from Earth took three days. The rocket that launched them, the Saturn V, was 111 metres tall, as tall as a 36-storey building. Around 600 million people watched on television.
pages.cap: The Saturn V rocket lifts off. It was the most powerful rocket of its time.
pages.fact: Did you know? The Apollo computer had far less memory than one photo on a phone today.

p: The Apollo astronauts did not come home empty-handed. They carried back 382 kilograms of Moon rock and dust. That is as heavy as five grown-ups.
Scientists still study those rocks today. They found no signs of life. The rocks are very old, some more than 4 billion years. They are older than almost any rock on Earth.
pages.cap: Moon rocks are kept in special clean rooms so nothing from Earth gets on them.
pages.fact: Did you know? In 2020 a Chinese probe brought back new Moon rocks, and in 2024 another brought the first rocks from the far side.

p: Every year, the Moon moves about 4 centimetres farther from Earth. That is about as fast as your fingernails grow.

We know because astronauts left mirrors on the Moon. Scientists bounce laser light off them and time the trip. Long ago the Moon was much closer and looked bigger. In the far future it will look a little smaller.
pages.cap: The Moon circles Earth, and its circle grows a tiny bit each year.
pages.fact: Did you know? When the Moon was young, a day on Earth lasted only about six hours.

pages.h: Try it: keep a Moon diary
p: Watch the Moon change shape.
steps: Get a notebook. Each clear night for two weeks, go outside at the same time.
Find the Moon. Draw its shape inside a circle.
Write the date and where it was in the sky.
After two weeks, look at your drawings in a row. Can you see the pattern?
If you miss a night because of clouds, just leave that circle blank.
pages.cap: Two weeks of drawings show the Moon growing from a thin crescent to full.
pages.safe: Go outside at night with a grown-up, and never look straight at the Sun.

pages.h: When the Moon hides the Sun
p: Sometimes the Moon moves right in front of the Sun. The day goes dark for a few minutes. This is a solar eclipse.

It works by luck. The Sun is 400 times wider than the Moon, but it is also 400 times farther away. So they look the same size in our sky. When the Moon passes through Earth's shadow instead, it turns a deep red. That is a lunar eclipse.
pages.cap: A shadow is a place the light cannot reach. Eclipses are giant shadows.
pages.fact: Did you know? Never look straight at the Sun, even in an eclipse. Special eclipse glasses keep your eyes safe.

opts: The Moon's pull on the oceans
pages.why: The Moon's gravity tugs on the sea, making the water rise and fall twice a day.

p: Near the Moon's poles are craters where the Sun never shines. They have been dark and freezing for billions of years.

Space probes have found water ice hiding in those shadows. This is a big deal. Astronauts could melt it to drink. They could even split it into fuel for rockets. That is one reason people want to land near the south pole next.
pages.cap: Water on the Moon stays frozen solid in craters that never see the Sun.
pages.fact: Did you know? In 2023, India's Chandrayaan-3 became the first lander to touch down near the Moon's south pole.

p: People are planning to walk on the Moon again. NASA's Artemis program aims to land astronauts near the south pole in the next few years. China plans a landing by 2030.
This time the plan is to stay longer and build a base. Astronauts would live in shelters, dig for ice and learn how to live on another world. Someday, that could help people reach Mars.
pages.cap: From the Moon, Earth looks like a blue marble hanging in the dark.
pages.fact: Did you know? Canada is building the robot arm for the new Moon station. It is called Canadarm3.

p: Some animals use the Moon. Dung beetles roll their dung balls in a straight line by watching the Moon's light.

Corals on the Great Barrier Reef all lay their eggs on the same few nights after a full moon. The sea fills with pink clouds of eggs. Sea turtles hatch at night and crawl towards the brightest light, which should be the Moon on the water.
pages.cap: Corals spawn together after a full moon.
pages.fact: Did you know? Some moths fly in a straight line by keeping the Moon on the same side of their body.

p: Earth has one moon. Some planets have none. Mercury and Venus have no moons at all.

Jupiter has more than 90 moons, and Saturn has more than 270. The biggest moon of all is Jupiter's Ganymede, which is bigger than the planet Mercury. Our Moon is the fifth-biggest moon in the whole Solar System. Not bad for a small planet.
pages.cap: Jupiter, with its red spot, has more than 90 moons swirling around it.
pages.fact: Did you know? Saturn's moon Titan has lakes, but they are full of liquid methane, not water.

What do you think it would feel like to jump six times higher than you can now?
Why do you think people want to go back to the Moon after so many years?
